extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, historians, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and analysis of the conditions that sustain or threaten democratic institutions (laws, manners, social structures) with comparative attention to the United States and European polities. Emphasis on practical remedies, social habits, and the roles of intermediate bodies and racial groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws and manners as the principal supports of democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether laws and manners are sufficient to maintain democratic institutions in countries besides America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asserts the success of American democratic institutions is more intimately connected with laws and manners than with the nature of the country; the central question is if the same causes (laws and manners) would of themselves produce the same results elsewhere. Note caution: lack of exact comparators makes conclusions tentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish American institutions from democratic institutions generally
rubrics_metrics.description: A careful distinction must be made between the institutions of the United States and democratic institutions in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the American form is the only or the best democratic model; other democratic organizations (including more centralized forms) may be conceivable and successful. Assess whether observed American features are particular applications rather than universal prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible democratic centralization with retained citizen participation
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic nation might be organized differently — more centralized — yet still have citizens participate within their sphere and possess certain rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider models where the majority consents to invest a family or individual with executive prerogatives for order and stability, while preserving citizen rights and participation in a limited sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws can (and should) be improved to enable democracy in less-favored countries
rubrics_metrics.description: American laws are not perfect; better laws might enable democratic institutions to succeed in countries less favored by natural circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legal design: identify defects in existing laws and imagine alternative legal frameworks that could substitute for advantageous physical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners, religion, and public opinion as moral restraints on power
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion, affections, sense of honor, family pride, provincial prejudices, custom, and public opinion limit arbitrary authority and confine power within effective barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the strength and persistence of social mores and beliefs as informal checks on rulers; note that erosion of these elements increases susceptibility to despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal/local laws as a means to channel democratic passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal laws restrain the ambition of citizens within a narrow sphere and turn passions that could harm the state to the good of the township or parish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the role of local institutions in absorbing and directing popular energies, opposing excessive envy, and providing practical experience that counters theoretical ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual introduction and infusion of democratic manners is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic institutions should be prudently introduced into society so they gradually mix with habits and are infused into the opinions of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reforms for gradualism: abrupt transplantation risks failure; success depends on socialization of new habits and opinions over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural advantages of the country cannot substitute for laws and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the country is not an adequate substitute for well-designed laws and cultivated manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating prospects for democracy, do not rely solely on favorable geography or physical circumstances; legal and moral instruments must be analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erosion of religion and traditional barriers increases risk of arbitrary power
rubrics_metrics.description: Since religion has lost empire over souls and long revolutions have destroyed respect for rulers, the visible and invisible barriers that once checked tyranny are weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether religion, local customs, and traditional intermediaries remain as constraints; their decline signals greater ease for rulers to exercise arbitrary power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogenization and loss of intermediate bodies facilitate collective oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: When provinces, towns, nobility, corporations, and local immunities disappear or are subordinated to uniform laws, it becomes as easy to oppress the whole as it was to oppress parts formerly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the existence and vitality of intermediate bodies (nobility, corporations, local privileges); their presence distributes power and represents opinion, reducing ease of centralized oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family feeling, honor, and aristocratic traditions as bulwarks against tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Family ties, honor, and the power (even moral) of aristocracy and corporations provided opposition to oppression; their weakening reduces organized resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure social linkages — family, clan, hereditary networks — and their capacity to sustain opposition to arbitrary authority when legal protections fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer democracy to despotism when no stable medium exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If societies face only two alternatives — leveling by democracy or leveling by despotic power — it is preferable to choose leveling by free institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance for policy: given the perpetual caprices and imperfect laws of democracy, these are still preferable to absolute monarchy or single-arm tyranny when intermediate regimes are impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political education and experience are essential but hard to supply
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to associate a people in government and still more difficult to supply them with the experience and feelings required to govern well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating readiness for self-government, analyze mechanisms for civic education, accumulation of political experience, and inculcation of governing habits; absence makes democratic governance fragile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial composition and treatment shape democratic prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence and treatment of distinct races (whites, negroes, Indians) in the same territory create social cleavages whose different conditions affect the destiny of the democratic people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess integration policies, social barriers erected by law and custom, and the prospects of amalgamation vs. persistent separation; failures risk social instability and weaken democratic cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery and servitude undermine capacity for liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery brutalizes the negro and robs him of the habits and capacities necessary for liberty; emancipation without the requisite experience may be destructive rather than liberating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the social and moral effects of servitude on an enslaved population and the supports required (education, property, institutions) to make freedom viable post-emancipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For indigenous peoples, war or genuine civilization were escape routes; current policies doom them
rubrics_metrics.description: The savages of North America had only two ways of escaping destruction: war or civilisation. They can no longer make war effectively, and they often refused or cannot now accept civilization — forced migrations produce misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering policies toward indigenous populations, assess whether assimilation paths, protection of traditions, or autonomous institutions exist; forced removal and inconsistent state/federal policies produce decline and barbarization.
